focus_area_title: Tips for Supporting One Another to Ensure Patient Safety
content_text_body:
In order to ensure patient safety, healthcare professionals need to trust one another, work together as a team, communicate, and support one another. Support for one another can mean several things like speaking up when you need assistance or closely monitoring your teammates to ensure they're not getting overwhelmed.  

### Why is it important?

Poor communication and teamwork are some of the leading causes of medical errors and patient safety events. According to Aiken and others, feeling supported within a nursing unit is a key factor in nursing satisfaction, intention to remain in the job, and the ability to provide safe patient care. Furthermore, Bridges and other researchers at the University of North Carolina found that team training and education on mutual support - a learning module of the TeamSTEPPSÂ® training developed by the Department of Defense and Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality - helped improve nursing ratings of teamwork significantly.    

On the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's (AHRQ's) website there is robust information regarding TeamSTEPPSÂ®. Below is a description of and information on Mutual Support, one of the key components of the TeamSTEPPSÂ® curriculum. **Below are several tips on how to be more supportive of one another in a care setting.**
 
#### Start with the Fundamentals

It's important to note that you can only support your teammates through consistent situation monitoring, or understanding what is going on around you and to your teammates. Furthermore, support happens information is communicated to one another (e.g., asking for help or offering support) and it's enhanced by leaders who encourage and role model support behaviors.  

#### Task Assistance

Mutual support occurs when teammates assist each other, provide and receive feedback, and demonstrate assertive and advocacy behaviors when patient safety is threatened. In regards to task assistance, teammates foster a climate in which it is expected that assistance will be actively sought and offered as a method for reducing the occurrence of error.

#### Providing Effective Informal Feedback

Increasing daily and informal feedback will help team members learn and improve. Effective informal feedback is timely, respectful, and specific. Furthermore, it's directed at improvement (i.e., helps prevent the same problems from happening again) and is considerate.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     

#### Advocacy and Assertion

In a mutually supportive environment, teammates must advocate for the patient when their viewpoint doesn't coincide with that of a decision-maker. They then must assert a corrective action in a firm and respectful manner. It is recommended that the advocate challenge the decision-maker twice if the initial assertion is ignored. The member being challenged must acknowledge the advocate. If the situation is still unresolved, any team member can "stop the line" calling for a stop to all procedures until the potential safety breach is worked through and resolved.
